prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for B006 to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The chair asks for one sentence on why this is a different discovery from the 2016 prize, and mine is this: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and integer quantum Hall-type invariants that rely on broken time reversal or on one-dimensional chains, whereas Kane and Mele showed that a time-reversal-invariant band insulator with spin-orbit coupling carries a Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states, with no magnetic field at all, and Molenkamp's HgTe wells showed those edge channels in transport. That is a new class of matter, not a further application of the old concept, and it is why the idea migrated into 3D materials, photonics and the search for Majorana modes. The pairing of the decisive theory with its first clean experiment, nearly twenty years of independent confirmation, and the consequence across several subfields remain unmatched on the shortlist. As a string theorist I cannot test the metrology or circuit arguments directly, so I weigh what I can judge: conceptual originality, stability of the interpretation, and the clarity of the credit. On citation wording, to avoid implying that the 3D materials discovery is honoured, the text should name the Z2 insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and the HgTe quantum-well observation, and nothing about three-dimensional topological insulators.
statement.case_against: The cost I cannot argue away is attribution. Hasan and the first 3D photoemission observations, the HgTe proposers Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (Zhang deceased) and the 3D theory of Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy all go unrecognised, and the citation must be honest that it covers the 2D discovery. A narrow citation protects the trio but openly leaves the 3D materials story to others. The 2016 overlap is a real concern for some colleagues even though I think the physics is distinct, and the committee may also prefer a candidate in a subfield not recently honoured. If Mele's omission turned out to be judged less costly than Hasan's, the Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan version would still be defensible, but I no longer prefer it.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the 2005 Kane-Mele papers are the single decisive step, that Hasan's 3D claim is partly carried by Kane and Mele through the Fu-Kane-Mele theory, and that the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio is the coherent core.
responses.response: I agree and I have not been given a reason to move since round 1. Your point that the 3D observation of Bi-Sb was itself a test of a Fu-Kane-Mele prediction is the strongest way to see why the trio does not erase the 3D story completely. Where I would still hold you to account is the citation: if Hasan's contribution is said to be carried by the theory credit, the wording must not suggest the committee is deciding the 3D priority question between Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3, which I regard as contested. A citation limited to the Z2 insulator, the quantum spin Hall state and HgTe handles this.

responses.point: Olsson, who opened with the same Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan trio as I did, now says the 2D quantum spin Hall discovery is the cleaner, singly attributable discovery and that a narrow defensible citation is better than a broad contested one.
responses.response: We have travelled the same path and I think correctly. Your phrase that the prize must name the discovery is the criterion I now apply: the 2D theory and its first experimental observation can be named exactly, whereas the 3D discovery has several competing originators and materials. I also take your point that the interpretation has been stable for two decades, which for a theorist is what separates a discovery from a fashion. I do not want the narrowness to be a pretext, so I will say plainly that this is a judgment about defensible credit, not a judgment that Hasan's work is minor.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, adopting the principle of theory plus first realisation, and says leaving out a co-author of the foundational papers is harder to defend than leaving out a later adjacent experiment.
responses.response: I accept that principle and I think it is the right test for this prize. It also answers your question to me in round 1: I do not hold that the 3D result is the decisive experimental confirmation, since the 2007 HgTe transport measurement came first and tests the Kane-Mele prediction directly. I would only add that it should be applied consistently, so if the committee ever faces a case where the first realisation is itself contested, the same rule should be spelled out again and not assumed.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B006 as first alternative, but says an exclusion of Mele or of the 3D discovery would be contested in a way the two-person clock prize would not, and that strong opening support is not an attribution that can be defended.
responses.response: That is a fair objection to the earlier Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan versions, and it is partly why I moved. With Kane and Mele both in, the prize no longer splits a joint result, and the remaining omissions (Hasan and the HgTe proposers) are a matter of the three-person ceiling and not an inconsistency in the credit. I hope the answer on 2016 above resolves the overlap worry you raised, but I cannot decide it for you. I also agree with you that support counts, including the six of eight here, are partly convergent and are not evidence by themselves.

responses.point: Kroll argues that magic-wavelength trapping is a new principle and not tuning, that the redefinition of the second should not delay the prize, and that B047 has the cleanest attribution on the list.
responses.response: Your explanation changed my view on one thing: I had read the lattice clock as a refinement of accuracy, and your account of why many neutral atoms can be interrogated with no first-order light shift persuades me that it is a distinct invention and not simply better spectroscopy. That is why B047 now replaces B038 as my second alternative. It does not change my ordering, because I judge the Z2 insulator to be the more far-reaching new phenomenon, but it is a genuine serious candidate and I would not object to it for a later year. I agree that waiting for the redefinition of the second would be the wrong criterion.

responses.point: Eriksson moved his first choice from B017 to B006 and keeps B017 as his first alternative, treating the unresolved pairing mechanism as a reason B017 can wait but not as a rejection.
responses.response: I agree with the reasoning and we now line up on B017. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is the best prediction-to-experiment story among the newer candidates, and I keep it as my first alternative. The unresolved mechanism of the superconductivity does not make it unconfirmed, but it means the interpretive core is still moving, and Kroll adds that Cao and Dean are absent from the credited names. I would revisit it in a year or two.

responses.point: Johansson accepts the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio, says he could live with my earlier cut, and now judges a second superconducting-circuit prize after 2025 hard to justify while disclosing his own interest in B038.
responses.response: I appreciate the declaration, and I do not think the disclosure needs to affect weighting beyond what you have already done by discounting your own enthusiasm. I have dropped B038 from my alternatives for the reasons we both gave: it is an enabling architecture whose scientific content is partly adjacent to the 2025 prize, and the omission of Girvin leaves the theory credit incomplete. I would not rule it out for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues who worry about the 2016 prize accept the distinction in time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling, which I cannot settle for them.

Whether the committee can live with omitting Hasan and the HgTe proposers Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang under a three-person ceiling, and whether the citation wording is enough to avoid claiming the 3D discovery.
Whether the lattice-clock case really is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes; I am relying on the arguments of Kroll and Lindroth and cannot test them independently.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene will be settled soon enough to move B017 ahead in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is a credited name on any shortlisted candidate. My own research is in string theory and cosmology, so I am an outsider to every shortlisted subject and defer to specialists on technical details. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
